blocks.prompt: The Llama Says No
blocks.text: A llama lives high up in the mountains. It has two toes on each foot with a soft pad underneath, so it walks quietly over the rocks. A llama talks by humming. A mom hums to her baby. The baby hums back. A baby llama is called a cria. Say it like this: KREE-uh. Llamas carry heavy bags for people. But a llama knows when a bag is too heavy. If you pile on too much, it just lies down in the dirt. It will not get up until you take some off. And if another llama pushes in at dinner, a llama can spit.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Says No
blocks.text: High in the Andes Mountains of South America, the air is thin and the ground is steep. Not many animals can work up there. The llama can. A llama stands about as tall as a grown person, and it will carry a load on its back for miles, day after day, along trails far too narrow and too steep for a cart. Its feet help. Instead of hard hooves, a llama has two toes and a soft leathery pad, so it grips the rock and does not chew up the trail. Here is the part people love best. A llama will not be tricked into carrying too much. Pile on more than about a quarter of its own weight, and the llama simply stops. It lies down in the dirt. It might hum, or groan, or spit. It will not stand up again until the load is lighter. People sometimes call that stubborn. It is not. It is a limit, and the llama keeps it. For thousands of years, the people of the Andes have worked with that rule instead of against it. They pack the llama fairly, and the llama walks.

blocks.prompt: An Empire With No Horses
blocks.text: The Inca ruled the largest empire in the Americas. It stretched about two thousand five hundred miles down the western edge of South America, tied together by tens of thousands of miles of stone road. Messengers ran those roads. Armies marched them. Food and cloth and salt moved along them constantly. And the Inca did all of it without a single horse. There were no horses in the Americas then, and no oxen, no donkeys, no animal anywhere on the continent strong enough to pull a plow or a cart. There was the llama. Andean people had already been living with llamas for thousands of years by then, since herders first tamed them from wild guanacos high in the mountains. A llama cannot pull. It carries. Herders drove caravans of hundreds of animals at a time, each one loaded with about sixty to a hundred pounds, up switchbacks that climbed past fifteen thousand feet where no wheel would have been any use at all. The llama gave more than transport. Its fiber was spun into cloth. Its dung dried into fuel in a landscape with almost no trees, and fed the fields as fertilizer. Its meat was cut into strips and dried for the road, a food the Quechua people called ch'arki. Spanish speakers borrowed that word, and English borrowed it again. We say jerky. So when people picture the Inca roads, they should picture the llama. Not as a curiosity, but as the engine.

blocks.prompt: The Camel That Went South
blocks.text: The llama is a camel. Not a cousin of a camel, not a camel-like animal, but a member of the camel family, and its history is stranger than the hump would suggest. The family did not begin in Arabia, and it did not begin in Peru. It began in North America roughly forty million years ago and stayed there for most of its existence, evolving through dozens of forms across the plains of what is now the United States. Then the continents shifted. When the Isthmus of Panama rose from the sea and joined North and South America, one branch of the family walked south into the Andes and became the guanaco, the vicuna, and eventually the llama and the alpaca. Another branch crossed the land bridge at Beringia into Asia and became the camels of the Gobi and the Sahara. Around twelve thousand years ago, the original North American camels disappeared entirely. The family survives only in the two places it wandered off to. Every llama in Peru and every camel in Egypt descends from an American animal with no American relatives left. Its body carries the record of that journey. Camelid blood is unlike any other mammal's: the red cells are oval rather than round, and they are small and tough, which lets thick blood move through fine vessels without jamming. Camelid hemoglobin also grips oxygen more tightly than ours does. Put those together and you get an animal that grazes calmly at fifteen thousand feet while a visiting human sits down with a headache. The feet finished the job. A llama walks on two toes over a soft pad, not a hard hoof, so it holds a steep rock trail and leaves the ground intact behind it. Add a body that will haul about a quarter of its own weight and then refuse the next pound, and the Andes had, waiting for them, exactly the animal the mountains required. Herders tamed the guanaco somewhere around five thousand years ago. Everything that followed in the high Andes, the roads, the caravans, the cloth, the empire, was built on the back of an animal whose ancestors once grazed in Nebraska.

6.title: The Llama That Carried an Empire
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Llama That Carried an Empire

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Lama glama, domesticated from the wild guanaco
Camelids evolved in North America and went extinct there
Pack animal, not a draft animal: it carries, it cannot pull
Oval red blood cells, unique among mammals
Camelids make heavy-chain-only antibodies
Nanobodies were found in camelid blood in 1989

blocks.prompt: The Underestimated Animal
blocks.text: Nobody takes the llama seriously. It has a face built for cartoons, ears shaped like two peeled bananas, and a public reputation resting almost entirely on spitting at tourists. That reputation has done the animal a disservice, because the llama is one of the most consequential animals in human history, and it currently sits near the center of a quiet revolution in medicine. Start with where it came from. The camel family did not originate in Arabia or in Peru. It originated in North America around forty million years ago and remained there for most of its history. Only in the last few million years, when the Isthmus of Panama rose and joined the two American continents, did one branch walk south into the Andes and become the guanaco, the vicuna, the alpaca, and the llama. A second branch crossed the Beringia land bridge into Asia and became the camels of the Gobi and the Sahara. Then, roughly twelve thousand years ago, the original North American camels vanished. The family survives only in its two exiles. Every llama in Peru and every camel in Egypt descends from an animal whose homeland now has none. Next, consider what the llama made possible. Before Europeans arrived, the Americas had no horses, no oxen, no donkeys, and no animal capable of pulling a plow or a cart. The Inca nonetheless built an empire running some two thousand five hundred miles down the spine of a continent, and they moved its freight on the backs of llamas. Caravans of hundreds of animals carried maize, salt, dried fish, and cloth along stone roads that climbed past fifteen thousand feet. A llama will carry roughly a quarter of its body weight and not one pound more. Overload it, and it lies down and refuses. That is not stubbornness. It is a hard limit, and Andean herders planned around it rather than fighting it, which may be the most sensible relationship any people have ever had with a working animal. The llama also supplied fiber for cloth, dung for fuel and fertilizer in a landscape with almost no trees, and dried meat the Quechua called ch'arki, a word that traveled through Spanish into English as jerky. The altitude should have defeated it. It did not, because camelid blood is built differently. Their red cells are oval rather than round, unlike those of any other mammal, small and durable enough to push through narrow vessels, and their hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than ours. Where a visitor gasps, a llama grazes. And then there is the discovery nobody went looking for. In 1989, researchers in Brussels examining camelid blood found antibodies with a structure no textbook described. Human antibodies are assembled from two kinds of protein chain. These were missing one kind entirely, and worked anyway. The business end of such an antibody can be cut away and used on its own. Scientists call these fragments nanobodies. They are a fraction of the size of a conventional antibody, considerably tougher, and, because they are small, able to reach into grooves on a virus or a protein where a normal antibody simply cannot fit. Llamas became the preferred animal for raising them, and the first nanobody medicine approved for human patients was developed from antibodies made in a llama. So: a living fossil of a lost American lineage, the engine of an empire built without wheels, an elegant solution to thin air, and now a small biological factory turning out a new class of drugs. The spitting is real. It is also, by some distance, the least interesting thing about the animal.
